Training PayGuard once by hand is easy. Retraining it every month, testing it, comparing it with the live model and shipping it without mistakes is hard. **MLOps** applies DevOps habits (automation, testing, monitoring) to machine learning, with one extra twist: the **data** changes too, so models must be retrained and re-validated, not just re-deployed ([Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/mlops-continuous-delivery-and-automation-pipelines-in-machine-learning)).

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- The three MLOps maturity levels and what each one automates
- The stages of a training pipeline, shown as an animation
- How data validation stops bad data before it reaches a model
- How experiment tracking and a quality gate decide what ships
:::

{{< include ../_series-nav.md >}}

## Three levels of maturity

Google describes three levels: **level 0, manual process**; **level 1, ML pipeline automation** (continuous training); and **level 2, CI/CD pipeline automation** (the pipeline code itself is tested and deployed automatically) ([Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/mlops-continuous-delivery-and-automation-pipelines-in-machine-learning)).

| Level | Who retrains | How often | Typical risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 Manual | A data scientist runs a notebook | A few times a year | Stale model, steps forgotten |
| 1 Pipeline | A scheduled or triggered pipeline | Weekly or monthly | Pipeline code changes are untested |
| 2 CI/CD | Pipeline code is tested and released like software | On every change | Higher setup effort |

: MLOps maturity levels {#tbl-levels}

Why does it matter? The simulation below follows PayGuard for a year while fraud patterns slowly change. The manual team retrains twice; the pipeline retrains every month.

```{python}
#| label: fig-levels
#| fig-cap: "Simulated model quality over a year. Automated monthly retraining keeps the model close to its best."
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np, plotly.graph_objects as go
from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
days = np.arange(365)
def quality(retrain_days):
    q, last = [], 0
    for d in days:
        if d in retrain_days: last = d
        q.append(0.93 - 0.00045 * (d - last) - 0.0000012 * (d - last) ** 2 + rng.normal(0, 0.004))
    return np.array(q)
manual = quality({0, 180})
auto = quality(set(range(0, 365, 30)))
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=days, y=manual, name="Level 0: manual, twice a year", line=dict(color=COLORS["rose"], width=2.5))
fig.add_scatter(x=days, y=auto, name="Level 1: pipeline, monthly", line=dict(color=COLORS["teal"], width=2.5))
fig.update_layout(height=380, xaxis_title="Day", yaxis_title="AUC on live data", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.12))
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

Averaged over the year, the automated model scores **`{python} f"{auto.mean():.3f}"`** AUC against **`{python} f"{manual.mean():.3f}"`** for the manual one. In fraud detection, that gap is money.

## Anatomy of a training pipeline

A pipeline is a chain of steps where each step must pass before the next one starts.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart TD
  A[Ingest<br/>new payments] --> B{Validate<br/>data}
  B -- fail --> X[Stop and alert]
  B -- pass --> C[Build<br/>features] --> D[Train] --> E[Evaluate]
  E --> F{Quality<br/>gate}
  F -- worse than live --> Y[Keep current model]
  F -- better --> G[Register<br/>new version] --> H[Deploy<br/>canary]
```

Press play to run the pipeline. Then tick "inject a bad data batch" and run it again: validation catches the problem before any training happens.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {ms, msStyle} from "/assets/js/ms-plot.js"
viewof bad = Inputs.toggle({label: "Inject a bad data batch", value: false})
viewof runs = Inputs.button("Run pipeline")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
steps = ["Ingest", "Validate", "Features", "Train", "Evaluate", "Gate", "Register", "Deploy"]
progress = {
  runs; bad;
  for (let t = 0; t <= steps.length * 12; t++) { yield t; await Promises.delay(40); }
}
{
  const W = 780, bw = 84, gap = (W - 20 - bw * steps.length) / (steps.length - 1);
  const failAt = bad ? 1 : -1;
  const cur = Math.floor(progress / 12);
  const state = i => failAt >= 0 && i > failAt ? "skip" : i < cur ? (i === failAt ? "fail" : "done") : i === cur ? (i === failAt ? "fail" : "run") : "wait";
  const col = {done: ms.teal, run: ms.amber, fail: ms.rose, wait: "currentColor", skip: "currentColor"};
  const msg = failAt >= 0 && cur > failAt ? "Stopped at validation: 12% of rows have a negative amount and 'hour' is missing. No model was trained. Alert sent."
    : cur >= steps.length ? "Pipeline passed. Version 14 registered and sent to a 5% canary."
    : `Running: ${steps[Math.min(cur, steps.length - 1)]}`;
  return htl.html`<div>${htl.svg`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} 110" style="width:100%;max-width:${W}px;font-family:Inter,system-ui,sans-serif">
    ${steps.map((s, i) => { const st = state(i), x = 10 + i * (bw + gap); return htl.svg`<g>
      ${i < steps.length - 1 ? htl.svg`<line x1="${x + bw}" y1="45" x2="${x + bw + gap}" y2="45" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="2"/>` : ""}
      <rect x="${x}" y="20" width="${bw}" height="50" rx="10" fill="${col[st]}" fill-opacity="${st === "wait" || st === "skip" ? 0.07 : 0.85}" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.2"/>
      <text x="${x + bw / 2}" y="50" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="${st === "wait" || st === "skip" ? "currentColor" : "white"}" opacity="${st === "skip" ? 0.35 : 1}">${s}</text>
      <text x="${x + bw / 2}" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.7">${st === "done" ? "passed" : st === "run" ? "running" : st === "fail" ? "failed" : st === "skip" ? "skipped" : ""}</text></g>`; })}
  </svg>`}<div class="ms-readout"><span>Status</span><b style="font-size:1rem">${msg}</b></div></div>`;
}
```

## Data validation in practice

Most pipeline failures start with data, not code. A few simple checks catch the common ones. Here is a real check on a simulated batch where something went wrong upstream.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
batch = pd.DataFrame({
    "amount": rng.lognormal(3.5, 1, 1000),
    "hour": rng.integers(0, 24, 1000).astype(float),
    "km_from_home": rng.exponential(15, 1000),
})
batch.loc[:119, "amount"] *= -1          # an upstream bug flips signs
batch.loc[500:540, "hour"] = np.nan      # a broken field

rules = {
    "amount > 0":        (batch.amount > 0).mean(),
    "hour not missing":  batch.hour.notna().mean(),
    "hour in 0..23":     batch.hour.dropna().between(0, 23).mean(),
    "km_from_home >= 0": (batch.km_from_home >= 0).mean(),
}
report = pd.DataFrame({"pass_rate": rules}).assign(
    ok=lambda d: d.pass_rate >= 0.99)
report.style.format({"pass_rate": "{:.1%}"})
```

Two rules fail, so the pipeline stops. Libraries such as **Great Expectations**, **Pandera** and **TFX Data Validation** turn these checks into reusable, documented suites.

## Experiment tracking: which run wins?

During tuning, a team may train dozens of versions. Tracking tools (MLflow, Weights & Biases) store each run's settings and scores, so the best one is easy to find and reproduce. Below are 40 simulated tuning runs.

```{python}
#| label: fig-runs
#| fig-cap: "Forty simulated tuning runs. Each dot is one training run; the star is the best by validation AUC."
#| code-fold: true
lr = 10 ** rng.uniform(-2.5, -0.3, 40)
depth = rng.choice([3, 5, 8, 12], 40)
auc_runs = 0.95 - 0.02 * (np.log10(lr) + 1.3) ** 2 - 0.0012 * (depth - 6) ** 2 + rng.normal(0, 0.003, 40)
best = int(np.argmax(auc_runs))
fig = go.Figure()
for d, c in zip([3, 5, 8, 12], [COLORS["slate"], COLORS["teal"], COLORS["indigo"], COLORS["violet"]]):
    m = depth == d
    fig.add_scatter(x=lr[m], y=auc_runs[m], mode="markers", name=f"max_depth {d}", marker=dict(size=10, color=c, opacity=0.85))
fig.add_scatter(x=[lr[best]], y=[auc_runs[best]], mode="markers", name="Best run",
                marker=dict(symbol="star", size=20, color=COLORS["amber"], line=dict(width=1, color="white")))
fig.update_layout(height=380, xaxis=dict(type="log", title="Learning rate"), yaxis_title="Validation AUC", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.14))
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

## The quality gate

A new model is promoted only if it is **at least as good as the live model** on the same held-out data, and not worse on any important slice (for example, small merchants or one country).

$$
\text{promote} \iff \text{AUC}_{\text{new}} \ge \text{AUC}_{\text{live}} - \varepsilon
\;\text{ and }\; \min_{s \in \text{slices}} \big(\text{AUC}^{(s)}_{\text{new}} - \text{AUC}^{(s)}_{\text{live}}\big) \ge -\delta
$$ {#eq-gate}

Here $\varepsilon$ is a small tolerance (say 0.002) and $\delta$ protects slices (say 0.01). Writing the gate as code removes arguments and gut feelings from the release decision.

## CI/CD for ML

At level 2, a push to the repository triggers tests, a training run and the gate. This GitHub Actions workflow is a compact starting point.

```{.yaml filename=".github/workflows/train.yml"}
name: train-and-gate
on:
  push: {branches: [main]}
  schedule: [{cron: "0 3 1 * *"}]   # also monthly, 03:00 on the 1st
jobs:
  pipeline:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: {python-version: "3.11"}
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest tests/                  # unit tests for feature code
      - run: python pipeline/validate.py    # data checks, exits 1 on failure
      - run: python pipeline/train.py       # logs run to MLflow
      - run: python pipeline/gate.py        # compares with live model
      - run: python pipeline/register.py    # only reached if gate passes
```

## Common pitfalls

| Pitfall | Fix |
|---|---|
| Training notebook and pipeline drift apart | Move code into a package; notebooks import it |
| No fixed random seeds or data snapshots | Log seed, data version and code commit with every run |
| Gate only checks the overall metric | Add slice checks and a latency check |
| Pipeline fails silently | Alert on failure and on "no run in 35 days" |

## Summary

- MLOps automates **training, testing and release**, because data keeps changing.
- Level 0 is manual, level 1 automates training, level 2 also tests and ships the pipeline itself.
- **Validate data first**, track every experiment, and let a **quality gate** decide what ships.
- Next: package everything so it runs anywhere with [Docker and containers](/deployment/containers/docker-for-ml.qmd).
